\chapter{Wi-Fi, Mobile Phones and Films}
\label{ch:wifi-movil-pelicula-apagar}
\hlchaptermodality{404}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can identify Wi-Fi, a mobile phone and a film, and ask someone to turn a phone off.}

Retrieve the four media words across hotel, phone and cinema scenes.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[apagar]{apagar — make the active thing quiet}

\label{lesson:ES-C404-apagar}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the telephone}. (\emph{El teléfono}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-pa-GAR}: keep all three \textbf{a} sounds clear and stress the final syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{apagar} — “to turn off” a device or light, and “to put out” a fire.

It continues Latin \textbf{pacāre}, “to calm or pacify.” The meaning moved from making something quiet to stopping its light, fire or activity. In the cinema, \textbf{apagar el teléfono} means “to turn off the phone.”
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{apagar}
  \item \emph{apagar el teléfono}
  \item \emph{por favor, apagar el teléfono}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{to turn off}. (\emph{Apagar}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/apagar}{DLE: apagar}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el wifi]{el wifi — the connection with a deliberately catchy name}

\label{lesson:ES-C404-wifi}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{internet}. (\emph{Internet}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item In much of the Spanish-speaking world you will hear \emph{WEE-fee}. \textbf{El wifi} is widely used; \textbf{la wifi} also occurs in parts of the Spanish-speaking world.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el wifi} — “the Wi-Fi” or “Wi-Fi.”

The name was coined to sound like \textbf{Hi-Fi}. The phrase \textbf{Wireless Fidelity} was attached afterward as marketing by the industry alliance and was later dropped. That history is why treating the phrase as the name's simple original expansion is misleading, while pretending the Alliance never used it also goes too far.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el wifi}
  \item \emph{¿Hay wifi?}
  \item \emph{wifi gratis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Ask whether there is Wi-Fi. (\emph{¿Hay wifi?})

Sources: \href{https://dle.rae.es/wifi}{DLE: wifi} and \href{https://boingboing.net/2005/11/08/wifi-isnt-short-for.html}{Phil Belanger's account of the naming}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el móvil]{el móvil — the phone named for moving}

\label{lesson:ES-C404-movil}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the telephone} and \emph{Wi-Fi}. (\emph{El teléfono, el wifi}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MO-vil}: the written accent keeps the stress on \textbf{mó}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el móvil} — “the mobile phone,” especially in Spain. Across much of Latin America, \textbf{el celular} is more usual.

Latin \textbf{mōbilis} meant “movable.” Spanish \textbf{teléfono móvil} is literally a mobile telephone; \textbf{el móvil} leaves the noun unstated because the movable device is understood.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el móvil}
  \item \emph{el teléfono móvil}
  \item \emph{apagar el móvil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{turn off the mobile phone}. (\emph{Apagar el móvil}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/m\%C3\%B3vil}{DLE: móvil}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la película]{la película — from a thin skin to a film}

\label{lesson:ES-C404-pelicula}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the cinema} and \emph{to begin}. (\emph{El cine, empezar}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pe-LEE-ku-la}: the written accent keeps the stress on \textbf{lí}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la película} — “the film” or “the movie.”

Latin \textbf{pellicula} meant a little skin, a diminutive of \textbf{pellis}, “skin.” A thin photographic layer, and then the strip coated with it, carried the word into cinema. The material's name became the movie's name.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la película}
  \item \emph{el cine y la película}
  \item \emph{la película empieza}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{the film begins}. (\emph{La película empieza}.)

Source: \href{https://dle.rae.es/pel\%C3\%ADcula}{DLE: película}.
\end{tcolorbox}
